articles.title: I Changed object to Lock and Stopped Paying the Monitor Tax
articles.description: The .NET 9 System.Threading.Lock type lets the same lock keyword skip Monitor. I benchmarked it: about 13% faster uncontended for a one-word field change, plus the caveat that it's still not for async.
articles.body_html:
I had a counter behind a lock that a profiler kept flagging, and I couldn't figure out why. The lock was basically never contended. One thread wrote to it almost all the time; the lock was there for the rare second writer that might show up. So I expected it to cost close to nothing. It didn't cost nothing. It cost about 24 nanoseconds every single acquire, and on a hot path that adds up to a line you can see in a flame graph.

The thing I'd stopped thinking about is what lock (someObject) actually compiles to. It's Monitor.Enter and Monitor.Exit wrapped in a try/finally, and Monitor hangs its state off the object's sync block. Even with no contention at all, you pay for that bookkeeping on every acquire and release. For years that was just the price of the lock keyword and there was nothing to do about it.

Since .NET 9 there is. There's a real type now, System.Threading.Lock, and the compiler special-cases it: if you lock on a variable whose type is Lock, it doesn't go through Monitor at all. It calls the type's own fast path instead. The part that surprised me is how little the code changes.

// before
private readonly object _gate = new();
lock (_gate) { _count++; }

// after
private readonly Lock _gate = new();
lock (_gate) { _count++; }   // same statement, different field type

One word. The lock statement is byte-for-byte identical. The only thing I changed is object to Lock on the field, and the compiler routes the whole thing through the new mechanism instead.

Making it tell on itself

I didn't want to trust a hunch, so I hammered both in the dullest way possible: one thread, a tight loop, fifty million lock-increment-unlock cycles, best of seven runs with the JIT already warm. This is a container with two cores, not a lab bench, so I care about the ratio between the two numbers, not the absolute nanoseconds.

for (long i = 0; i < Ops; i++)
{
    lock (objectGate) { c++; }   // object + Monitor
}

for (long i = 0; i < Ops; i++)
{
    lock (realLock) { c++; }     // System.Threading.Lock
}

Ops per trial: 50,000,000   Trials: 7 (reporting best)
Processors: 2   Server GC: False

Uncontended, single thread (best of 7):
  lock(object)          1230 ms   24.60 ns/op
  lock(Lock)            1084 ms   21.68 ns/op
  Lock.EnterScope()     1083 ms   21.66 ns/op
  speedup vs object:  1.13x

So about 13% off every uncontended acquire, for changing one word. I'll be honest about the size of that: 13% of 24 nanoseconds is three nanoseconds. If your lock gets taken a few hundred times a second, you will never, ever notice this, and you shouldn't go rewriting working code to chase it. Where it starts to matter is the hot inner path that grabs a lock millions of times, and in that spot three nanoseconds times millions is a real slice of a frame.

I also ran the contended case, two threads actually fighting over the same lock, and the gap narrowed to about 1.05x. That tracks. Once threads are genuinely blocking each other, the cost is dominated by the waiting, not by the per-acquire overhead, so the fast path has less room to help. The uncontended path is where the new type earns its keep, which is lucky, because uncontended is what most locks are most of the time.

The explicit form, and what it buys

If you'd rather not use the lock statement, the type gives you a scope you dispose:

using (realLock.EnterScope())
{
    _count++;
}

EnterScope() returns a ref struct called Scope. That's not a detail to skim past. A ref struct can't be boxed, can't be stored in a field, can't escape to the heap, so you physically cannot hold onto the scope past the block it lives in. The object-plus-Monitor pattern never gave you that guarantee; you could always forget an Exit or get clever and leak the hold. Here the compiler won't let you. My run clocked EnterScope() at the same speed as the statement, so there's no penalty for the clearer form.

The caveat that actually bit me

One thing caught me out, because I briefly thought the new type would save me from it and it doesn't. You still can't await while holding a Lock:

error CS1996: Cannot await in the body of a lock statement

That's not a new rule and it's not something the Lock type introduced. The exact same error fires on a plain lock (object) and always has. I mention it because when I first reached for Lock, some corner of my brain assumed a shiny new synchronization primitive might finally let me hold it across an await. Nope. A Lock is for short, synchronous critical sections, same as Monitor always was. If what you actually need is mutual exclusion around an await, that's still SemaphoreSlim with WaitAsync, and reaching for Lock there just gets you a compile error pointing at the real problem.

So my rule, and this is an opinion rather than a benchmark: for new code, I default to Lock now. It says what it means, it hands me a scope I can't misuse, and it's a hair faster for free. For existing code that works, I only swap it when I'm already in that file for another reason, or when the profiler put me there. Three nanoseconds is not worth a diff on its own.

The full benchmark

Here's the whole thing. It's a top-level program targeting net10.0 (the Lock type works on .NET 9+), so drop it in a fresh console project and dotnet run -c Release. The numbers above came from a 2-core container with workstation GC, so treat them as ratios, not absolutes.

using System.Diagnostics;

const long Ops = 50_000_000;    // lock/unlock pairs per trial
const int Trials = 7;

Console.WriteLine($"Ops per trial: {Ops:N0}   Trials: {Trials} (reporting best)");
Console.WriteLine($"Processors: {Environment.ProcessorCount}   Server GC: {System.Runtime.GCSettings.IsServerGC}");
Console.WriteLine();

// uncontended: object + Monitor (what lock(_gate) has always meant)
var objectGate = new object();
long objectBest = long.MaxValue;
for (int t = 0; t < Trials; t++)
{
    long c = 0;
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (long i = 0; i < Ops; i++)
        lock (objectGate) { c++; }
    sw.Stop();
    GC.KeepAlive(c);
    objectBest = Math.Min(objectBest, sw.ElapsedMilliseconds);
}

// uncontended: the new System.Threading.Lock
var realLock = new Lock();
long lockBest = long.MaxValue;
for (int t = 0; t < Trials; t++)
{
    long c = 0;
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (long i = 0; i < Ops; i++)
        lock (realLock) { c++; }   // same keyword, different field type
    sw.Stop();
    GC.KeepAlive(c);
    lockBest = Math.Min(lockBest, sw.ElapsedMilliseconds);
}

// the explicit EnterScope form
long scopeBest = long.MaxValue;
for (int t = 0; t < Trials; t++)
{
    long c = 0;
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (long i = 0; i < Ops; i++)
        using (realLock.EnterScope()) { c++; }
    sw.Stop();
    GC.KeepAlive(c);
    scopeBest = Math.Min(scopeBest, sw.ElapsedMilliseconds);
}

double ObjNs(long ms) => ms * 1_000_000.0 / Ops;

Console.WriteLine("Uncontended, single thread (best of 7):");
Console.WriteLine($"  lock(object)        {objectBest,6} ms   {ObjNs(objectBest):F2} ns/op");
Console.WriteLine($"  lock(Lock)          {lockBest,6} ms   {ObjNs(lockBest):F2} ns/op");
Console.WriteLine($"  Lock.EnterScope()   {scopeBest,6} ms   {ObjNs(scopeBest):F2} ns/op");
Console.WriteLine($"  speedup vs object:  {(double)objectBest / lockBest:F2}x");
Console.WriteLine();

// contended: several threads fighting over the same lock
static long RunContended(int threads, long perThread, Action<long> body)
{
    long best = long.MaxValue;
    for (int t = 0; t < 3; t++)
    {
        var tasks = new Thread[threads];
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        for (int k = 0; k < threads; k++)
        {
            tasks[k] = new Thread(() => body(perThread));
            tasks[k].Start();
        }
        foreach (var th in tasks) th.Join();
        sw.Stop();
        best = Math.Min(best, sw.ElapsedMilliseconds);
    }
    return best;
}

int nthreads = Math.Max(2, Environment.ProcessorCount);
long perThreadOps = 10_000_000;
long sharedCounter = 0;

var objGate2 = new object();
long objContended = RunContended(nthreads, perThreadOps, n =>
{
    for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) lock (objGate2) { sharedCounter++; }
});

var lockGate2 = new Lock();
long lockContended = RunContended(nthreads, perThreadOps, n =>
{
    for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) lock (lockGate2) { sharedCounter++; }
});

Console.WriteLine($"Contended, {nthreads} threads x {perThreadOps:N0} ops (best of 3):");
Console.WriteLine($"  lock(object)        {objContended,6} ms");
Console.WriteLine($"  lock(Lock)          {lockContended,6} ms");
Console.WriteLine($"  speedup vs object:  {(double)objContended / lockContended:F2}x");
Console.WriteLine($"  final counter:      {sharedCounter:N0}");

What's your rule for touching working lock code? Mine is "only when I'm already there," but I know people who'd rewrite the whole file on sight. Curious where you land.

— still benchmarking the stuff nobody filed a ticket for

articles.title: Autosave UX: Show What Saved Means in Your Public SaaS Demo
articles.description: To get useful feedback on autosave UX, show one edit moving from local text to a confirmed save, then...
articles.body_html:
To get useful feedback on autosave UX, show one edit moving from local text to a confirmed save, then show a failed save and its recovery. Reopen the same item at the end. A public demo should make clear which version is on screen, which version was accepted, and what the user can safely do next.

A smooth typing clip leaves the difficult part out. The text looks present because it is still in the editor. That alone does not demonstrate that it will survive reopening, reach another device, or remain after a failed request.

Building this sequence into a small public demo gives founder peers a concrete behavior to inspect. The question becomes whether the product tells the truth about the latest edit, rather than whether the animation looks polished.

Define what Saved promises in this product

Write a plain sentence before choosing the status label. Does saved mean the server accepted this revision? Does it mean a draft exists only on this device? Is there a separate publication step? Different products can make different promises, but the interface should not blur them.

For example, a draft editor might confirm that a revision has been accepted by the service while still requiring a separate action to publish it. The demo should show that boundary. A person should not infer that their writing is public just because it is saved, or safely stored remotely just because it remains visible.

Use wording that matches the actual implementation. If you only have a prototype with simulated responses, label it as a prototype. If the recording uses a controlled failure, say so. An honest demonstration of an unfinished state is more useful than a finished-looking badge with an undefined meaning.

Track revisions rather than the last response alone

Consider a fictional editor for a client brief. The sample text begins with Meeting on Tuesday. The user changes it to Meeting on Wednesday. Call that revision A. While its request is pending, they change it again to Meeting on Thursday, revision B.

A response confirming A does not confirm B. If the interface displays Saved while B is still pending, it gives the user an inaccurate account of their current text. The visible status needs to describe the revision they are looking at, not merely the most recent successful response.

This is a behavior to verify whatever tools or architecture you use. You can serialize updates, track revisions, or adopt another suitable approach. The public demonstration need not reveal private infrastructure or pretend that one design solves every concurrency case.

Write the expected outcome in your notes: when the confirmation for A arrives, the editor still shows that B needs saving. When B is accepted, the saved indication refers to B. That expectation is specific enough for someone else to challenge.

Show a pending save without stealing the typing task

The user should be able to understand that work is pending without being repeatedly pulled away from writing. Put the status near a stable part of the editor and keep the meaning consistent as the state changes.

The W3C explanation of status messages describes making relevant updates available to assistive technology without moving focus. Its examples cover waiting, results, and errors. It does not prescribe your autosave timing or prove that a particular component is accessible.

In your review, check the visible message and its announcement separately. A status that only changes color may be unclear to readers who cannot perceive that change. A screen reader user should not have to leave the editor and search for an update that matters to their next action.

Avoid announcing every keystroke. Review the actual announcement behavior with the tools and browsers you support. A screenshot of a label cannot establish how that experience works.

Use a controlled failed-save example

Use disposable sample content in a test environment. Make the failure observable and repeatable through your normal development tools or test controls. Explain what you are simulating and what you are not checking.

Return to the fictional client brief. Revision A has been saved. The user types revision B, and that save fails. The editor keeps B visible and identifies that the latest changes have not been saved. A retry action is available if the product supports one.

The status should not quietly return to a reassuring success state just because an older version exists. Tell the user about the unsaved changes. If the product can preserve only part of the work or has a recovery limit, make that limit visible rather than promising that nothing can be lost.

Record the sequence from before the edit through the failure. An isolated error screenshot cannot show whether the application discarded text, changed focus, or mislabeled the previous revision.

Retry the current edit and reopen the item

After a failure, the user may continue typing. Decide what your retry action sends. Does it retry the failed revision, or save the latest visible content? Either way, the behavior should be explicit and the resulting status should match the text it covers.

For the worked example, choose a simple expectation: Retry saves the current visible revision. The user adds a location to the brief, retries, and waits for confirmation. The reopened item should contain both the changed day and the added location.

Reopening is a useful check because it removes the comforting presence of the old editor session. Compare the actual content, not just a toast or a checkmark. Keep the test item identifiable so you do not accidentally inspect a different draft with similar text.

This is still a narrow test. A successful reopen in one environment does not establish behavior across devices, account permissions, offline sessions, or concurrent editors. Name those gaps if they matter to the product's promise.

Share a small trace alongside the public demo

A short written trace makes the clip easier to review. Include the starting text, the exact change, the controlled delay or failure, the status shown, the action taken, and the text found after reopening.

For a community discussion on Buildside, ask one focused question: after the failed save, would you know which changes were still at risk? A second useful question is whether the retry label accurately describes the action. Do not ask peers to certify the whole storage system from a short video.

Keep customer information out of the example. Sample text should be visibly ordinary and disposable. If the clip includes browser tools, crop unrelated tabs and private values while retaining the parts needed to understand the sequence.

Include text that explains the important states for readers who cannot watch the recording. The post should remain useful even when the media does not play.

Turn feedback into a behavior decision

Separate a reader's expectation from the application's observed behavior. Someone might expect a save confirmation to remain visible longer. That is a design question. A newer revision being marked saved before acceptance is a correctness problem. Treating both as vague feedback makes the next step harder to choose.

Keep a compact review note: what the person saw, what they expected, what the application actually did, and the change you will make or investigate. If the evidence is incomplete, record the missing step rather than guessing.

For a small release, verify a few meaningful paths: normal save, delayed save while typing continues, failure, retry after another edit, and reopening. Add concurrent editing or offline recovery checks when those are part of the product you offer. Match the scope to the actual promise.

Then publish the result with its limits. Say which paths you checked and which remain open. A clear autosave demo gives readers a way to inspect a real product decision, and gives you a more useful next task than another round of comments about how clean the editor looks.

articles.title: HTTP 206 and SEO: Inspect the Range Before Calling the HTML Complete
articles.description: When an HTML request returns HTTP 206, inspect the requested range and the bytes actually delivered...
articles.body_html:
When an HTML request returns HTTP 206, inspect the requested range and the bytes actually delivered before calling the page complete. Compare it with a request for the full document. A successful response can represent only part of a resource, so a green status alone does not tell you whether the buyer's answer arrived.

Treat this as a response-delivery investigation. The first goal is to explain what the public request received and why. A corrected response is useful technical evidence; it is not, by itself, proof of indexing or an AI citation.

Start with the request that produced 206

RFC 9110 defines 206 Partial Content as a successful response fulfilling a range request by transferring one or more parts of the selected representation. It says clients need to inspect Content-Type and Content-Range to understand which parts are enclosed.

Save the method, URL, request headers, status, response headers, and response body from the observation. Include the time and environment. Do not reduce the record to a screenshot of the status code, because the request may explain why the response contains a partial document.

Identify whether the request asked for a byte range. If a colleague used a diagnostic tool, ask for its request configuration too. A deliberately narrow request and an ordinary full-document request are different tests, even when they target the same URL.

Keep authorization material out of any broadly shared issue. The technical handoff should preserve the relevant range information without spreading session cookies or credentials. Use your team's normal controlled records for sensitive captures.

Compare the full request with the range request

Use an authorized inspection method to request the same public document without the range restriction. Preserve this response separately. Compare its status, content type, and body with the original observation rather than assuming that both tests retrieved the same representation.

For a single-part 206 response, the standard specifies a Content-Range header describing the enclosed range. Its total resource length and the response's Content-Length describe different things. Avoid treating the number of delivered bytes as the size of the complete page.

If the response contains multiple parts, read the relevant multipart structure instead of looking for one continuous HTML document. The standard covers that arrangement too. This distinction concerns HTTP semantics; it does not establish how a particular search product will use the response.

A useful comparison record has one row per request, with the request's range setting, resulting status, content type, and the location of the answer passage in the returned body. The rows should remain separate even if their URLs match exactly.

Work through a fictional missing-answer incident

Imagine a public export guide whose opening explains the feature, while a later section identifies which role can run the export. An engineer's diagnostic capture contains the opening but ends before the role restriction. The response status is 206.

In this fictional example, the diagnostic request explicitly asked for the first segment of the document. A second request without that range returns the complete guide, including the role restriction. These are invented conditions for a debugging exercise, not measured results from a real website.

The evidence supports a narrow conclusion: the first capture cannot establish that the public document omits the restriction. It intentionally retrieved an incomplete segment. The content editor should not rewrite the guide merely to satisfy a diagnostic record that never requested the full body.

Now change one assumption. Suppose an ordinary full-document request also receives that same short segment. The investigation changes. The team must trace why the public delivery path returns partial material for that request. That is a delivery question before it becomes a content-quality question.

This two-case exercise helps distinguish an incomplete observation from an incomplete delivery. Both can produce a record with missing text, but they require different next actions.

Trace the layer that changed the response

If the ordinary request receives an unexpected partial response, compare outputs through the delivery path your team controls. The application, proxy, content-delivery service, and cache configuration are possible places to investigate. The presence of a header alone does not identify which layer generated it.

Ask the responsible owner to explain any range handling, transformation, or caching rule that applies to the route. Compare the configuration with the captured request and response. Do not remove a broad shared policy simply because it contains a familiar header name.

For the fictional guide, the next useful finding might be a route-specific rule that incorrectly reuses a partial representation. That remains a hypothesis until the team traces the output. Document the uncertainty rather than presenting the most plausible explanation as a proven cause.

If other document types use intentional range requests, preserve their supported behavior. A repair for an HTML guide should not silently disable legitimate partial delivery for unrelated resources. Define the affected route family and the intended behavior before changing anything.

Verify the content that matters to the reader

After the relevant repair, repeat the original request and the full-document comparison. Confirm that each receives the intended representation. Check the opening, the disputed answer passage, and the end of the body, rather than stopping after the first screen looks reasonable.

In the fictional guide, the important check is whether the public full request includes the role restriction with the export instructions. The presence of a title and navigation is insufficient. A page can appear familiar while the sentence that determines eligibility is missing.

Keep the actual response captures with the issue. Record which request each capture belongs to. If someone later sees another 206 response, they can compare the circumstances without reopening the entire diagnosis from memory.

Also verify the normal browser experience after the repair. That complements the response check; it does not replace it. A browser's current state and a captured public request can expose different parts of a delivery problem.

Keep Google's documented scope clear

Google's HTTP status guidance says a 2xx response may be considered for processing and that a success code does not guarantee indexing. Its current table does not provide a separate 206-specific indexing promise.

Do not turn the general success category into a claim that Google will reconstruct or index every partial HTML response. Likewise, this guide makes no claim that ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini handles partial responses in the same way.

If you inspect a search-related observation, keep its evidence separate: the requested URL, tool or crawler identity, time, returned representation, and any reported indexing state. A manually constructed range request is not a captured Googlebot request merely because the guide concerns SEO.

This separation lets engineering close a verified delivery defect without promising a search outcome. Search follow-up can then use its own evidence and relevant product documentation.

Close the issue with a reproducible distinction

Write down whether the original problem came from the diagnostic request, the public delivery path, or an unresolved difference between the two. Include the before-and-after requests, relevant headers, complete-body checks, and responsible configuration owner.

State what was repaired and what remains unknown. If the first observation was simply partial by design, close that misunderstanding and keep the useful full-document capture. If delivery was wrong, document the specific corrected behavior and the route sample used to verify it.

The durable lesson is to make completeness an observable property of the returned document. A status code helps explain the response, but the actual request and body determine whether your inspection reached the answer you were trying to assess.
